steps.title: Two columns
paragraphs: Jordan had to write an essay: “Should our school have a four-day week?” Jordan’s first thought was “Yes! Longer weekends!” and nothing else.
So Jordan drew a line down a page. On the left, reasons FOR. On the right, reasons AGAINST.
For: more rest, fewer bus trips, time for family. Against: longer school days, parents need childcare, less time with friends.
Jordan looked at both columns and picked the side with the strongest reasons, not the side that sounded most fun. The against column even gave Jordan a counterclaim to answer.

cards.title: Brainstorm before you choose
cards.body: Write the question at the top. List every reason you can think of on BOTH sides, fast, without judging. Then circle the three strongest reasons on one side: the ones you can back up with a fact or an example.

cards.title: Choose the side you can prove
cards.body: Pick the side with the best evidence, even if it isn’t your first feeling. A strong reason is specific and can be checked: “Walking to school adds 20 minutes of exercise” beats “walking is good.”

cards.title: From brainstorm to thesis
cards.text:
Question: Should students have a longer lunch?
For: time to eat properly ✓, time to play and rest ✓, shorter lines ✓, more time to chat
Against: school ends later, less class time
Thesis: Schools should give students a longer lunch because they need time to eat properly, rest and avoid long lines.
Counterclaim to answer: Some people say a longer lunch means less class time.
cards.note: The three circled reasons become the three body paragraphs. The best against reason becomes the counterclaim.

prompts: Did brainstorming both sides change what you thought? How?
Which of your three reasons is the strongest? What evidence could prove it?
